I’m claiming the lower-right center with Blue. It blocks Yellow’s direct advance up column 4 and gives Green a chance to occupy (4,3), while avoiding the sandwich trap around Red’s advanced piece at (3,3).

{"move":{"from":{"row":4,"col":7},"to":{"row":4,"col":4}}}

```memo
### Position read
The opponent advanced Red from (0,3) to center (3,3). We moved Blue from (4,7) to the lower-right center (4,4). All losses remain zero.

### Our plan
Contest center immediately. If (4,3) remains open on Green’s turn, strongly consider Green (4,0)->(4,3), giving us both lower central squares. Otherwise develop Green to block the opponent’s center majority and build same-color sandwich flanks. Keep Blue (4,4) unless a concrete tactical move is stronger.

### Opponent tendencies
The opponent opened with an immediate central occupation, suggesting a center-focused plan.

### Lessons
Red at (3,3) makes (3,2) and (3,4) tactically dangerous for Blue: Red may land on the opposite side and sandwich-capture. Teammate colors never form capture flanks, and friendly pieces can be captured inside mixed sandwich lines.
```

```memo
The opponent holds (3,3) with Red and (4,3) with Yellow; we hold (4,4) with Blue. Green has advanced to (4,2), beside Yellow, with all losses still zero. The opponent controls two of four center squares but cannot complete center occupation while our Blue remains at (4,4).

### Our plan
Keep Blue (4,4) unless moving it enables a concrete tactic or is necessary to avoid capture. Use Green (4,2) as a same-color sandwich anchor: after safely clearing Blue from (4,4), seek to bring another Green onto (4,4) vertically and capture Yellow at (4,3). Contest (3,4) with Blue if practical, while watching for Red’s likely arrival there.

### Opponent tendencies
The opponent is pursuing rapid center occupation with both colors.

### Lessons
Green (4,2) and Blue (4,4) do not sandwich Yellow because teammate colors cannot flank together. Moving into a sandwich is safe; only a move by the potential capturer triggers captures.
```

Blue retreats one step down to preserve the threatened center piece while creating a useful vertical anchor. From (5,4), it can support future Blue sandwich captures if the opponent continues stacking pieces in column 4.

{"move":{"from":{"row":4,"col":4},"to":{"row":5,"col":4}}}

```memo
### Position read
All losses remain zero. The opponent holds center squares (3,3) with Red and (4,3) with Yellow; our Blue has withdrawn from (4,4) to (5,4), while Green remains at (4,2). Blue had to leave (4,4) because Yellow could land at (4,5) and sandwich it against Yellow (4,3).

### Our plan
Use Blue (5,4) as a vertical sandwich anchor. If the opponent occupies (4,4), Blue may capture from (3,4); if Red also stacks at (3,4), Blue may be able to land at (2,4) and capture the whole intervening chain. Keep contesting column 4 and avoid allowing all four center squares to remain opponent-occupied. Green should improve access toward the center while preserving (4,2) as a possible horizontal anchor.

### Opponent tendencies
The opponent is pursuing rapid center occupation and has advanced Red to (2,4), likely to support entry into (3,4).

### Lessons
Same-color anchors are tactically valuable even outside the center. Before occupying a center square, check whether the opponent can land beyond it using an existing same-color piece as the far flank.
```

```memo
### Lessons
```
```memo
When three center squares are already held, stopping immediate center completion overrides ordinary development. A forced blocker can buy a tempo even when it is capturable; evaluate the opponent’s landing square for a counterattack on the following allied turn.
```
